new_statements.quote: In 1972 when writing Biangai Phonemes, we considered the rhythm patterns as stress. [...] Stress was described as being manifested by intensity. "Stress does not significantly effect length of vowels. Primary stress occurs on the last or second last syllable of a stem. A stressless word or morpheme following a stem with no stress, gains stress on the first syllable. Secondary stress is predictable on the first syllable of a word. It occurs on the first and every alternate syllable preceeding stressed syllables, and /or on every alternate syllable following a stressed syllable." [...] Neither stress nor tone is phonemic and since it varies according to speakers it will not be written.

This source (repeating Dubert & Dubert 1972/73 p. 30 verbatim) says primary stress is on the last OR second-last syllable of the stem with no conditioning, that some stems have no primary stress, and its own examples put primary on the final syllable of 2-syllable 'pa"nu (catalog says initial, '10') and on the suffix in 'pilan"dik / 'wabene"mek (not penult). It further says stress is non-phonemic and varies by speaker, and that the three village groups differ in placement. Co…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress (marked " in the source's notation, with ' for secondary) falls on the last or the second-last syllable of the stem, with no rule given for which; some stems carry no primary stress at all, and then a following stressless morpheme takes stress on its first syllable. Examples p. 6: "mango / "mango'bek (stem-penult), 'pa"nu / 'pa"numale (stem-final), 'pilang / 'pilan"dik and 'wabeneng / 'wabene"mek (primary-less stems, suffix gains stress), 'lang / 'la"wek, "wak / "wa?pek. The 1981 authors then reframe the whole thing as village-group 'rhythm patterns' that are non-phonemic and speaker-variable and will not be.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress is predictable on the first syllable of the word and on every alternate syllable before the primary and/or every alternate syllable after it (p. 6, quoting 1972 p. 30).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 5: 'However, one could say there are 3 groups on the basis of rhythm patterns. The Ngowiye speakers have one rhythm pattern, and within the Yongolege there are two rhythm patterns. Elauru and Werewere villagers have a different rhythm pattern from Winima and Kwembu villagers. The people describe these as a different "neck".' The table on p. 5 marks the same phrases differently per group: talegi carries the acute on its final syllable in the Ngowiye and Kwembu/Winima columns but on ta- in the Werewere/Elauru column; Lawikmek has the acute on -wik- (Ngowiye) vs -mek (Werewere/Elauru), with hand-drawn pitch contours over each. p. 6: 'Neither stress nor tone is phonemic and since it varies according to speakers it will not be.' p. 13 (conclusion): 'one language with no dialects. The two or three groupings, as described, have features of word shortening, sound shifting, and rhythm'.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1972/73 stress description that the 1981 survey repeats was made for the Yongolege group 'with the help of two Werewere speakers' (Dialect Survey p. 6). The survey (p. 5) distinguishes Ngowiye villages (Wandumi, Kaisenik, Biawen) from Yongolege villages (Werewere, Elauru vs Kwembu, Winima) and says the three groups have different rhythm patterns while remaining 'one language with no dialects' (p. 13). Any placement statement for Biangai therefore rests on Werewere (Yongolege) speech.

readall_conflicts: The catalog's StressTyp2 record codes Biangai as fixed penultimate primary stress with initial/alternating secondary (stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 10010 (1 = a stressed syllable)). 6), quotes the Duberts' own 1972/73 statement that primary stress is on the last OR second-last syllable of the stem with no conditioning given, that some stems have no primary stress (a following morpheme then takes it), and its examples include stem-final primary in a disyllable ('pa"nu) and suffix-borne primary ('pilan"dik, 'wabene"mek), which the penult template does not generate. The same page adds that neither stress nor tone is phonemic and that it varies by speaker, and p. 5 reports three village groups with different 'rhythm patterns' (different placement of the acute/pitch peak on the same phrases). So the primary source and the catalog disagree on type (lexical stem-based vs fixed penult); the six other works (five discourse papers and the 1978 grammar) are silent. This agrees with our check note already attached to the webcat record (reclassify as lexical; drop the StressTyp2 penult template).
